newsitem.title: UK: London equity brokers scale back trading desks.
newsitem.headline: London equity brokers scale back trading desks.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange (LSE) is still a year from big changes to its 10-year-old share trading system, but some brokerages are already culling the ranks of highly-paid dealers who are at the heart of the current regime.

A statement this week from Merrill Lynch, one of London's top brokerages, that it was shedding 14 of its 64 market-making posts confirmed prolonged speculation about impending job cuts at leading broking houses.
The jobs cuts are minor in comparison with previous upheavals in London. After heavy loses at the end of the 1980's, some big houses withdrew from trading equities in London.

They are also minor in the context of the expanding operations of London investment banks. NatWest, for instance, set the eight market-making jobs it recently cut against 120 posts added in its equity operations this year.
But the reductions are a pointer to a significant change in Europe's leading financial centre as firms get ready for for the new order-driven trading environment.
"Culturally we have to get used to a different set of criteria," said one head of trading, who asked not to be named.
"We have got to start looking at how an order-driven system works and start building a relationship with clients, we can't just do it at the drop of a hat."
By this time next year, the LSE plans to phase in an automated trading system where brokers input buy and sell orders into a computer network instead of agreeing trades by phone.

The new "order-driven" system will potentially do away with the need for ranks of traders, the best earning between 100,000 ($156,400) and 200,000 pounds, that investment banks have employed since the Big Bang shakeup of the LSE in 1986.

"As we approach the introduction of an order book, numbers will come under more pressure because all the bargains are going to be matched automatically," said one senior trader. "Computer will just be talking to computer."

Michael Marks, co-head of global equities at Merrill Lynch, said this week's cuts "...anticipate the needs of our clients in the new trading environment and will enhance our ability to manage our continuing capital commitment to the market."

Merrill will still have the largest market-making team in London and naturally aims to retain its leading market position. But Marks said: "The fact is we have all got to restructure how we trade by the fourth quarter of 1997."
Other brokers have been taking similar measures. UBS said it had slimmed its market-making staff to 24 and SBC Warburg said it had cut about 14 jobs over the past year to leave 20.
NatWest and SBC said new in-house computer systems allowed them to trade the same number of stocks with fewer people. But it far from clear that all London brokerages will follow Merrill's lead.

"It would not surprise me if we need more not less people... if we are going to offer immediacy in large trades, which is what we want to provide to clients, we need the staff," one senior trader at a leading market-making house told Reuters.
BZW, Barclays' investment banking arm, said its staffing levels had been steady at 40 and it had no plans to reduce.
Nevertheless the Merrill move has sparked speculation of more job cuts to come.

"Not long ago we had market making teams of 60, 70 or 80 people at some firms and most big houses have been slowly cutting down," said a senior dealer at one U.S. investment bank. "This is giving a major boost to the reduction in numbers."

Job cuts are anyway not just related to the new trading system. "For all firms this is a very sensitive issue, it is always under review as we look to strengthen the firm and look for those who are underperforming," said another equities head. ($1=.6395 Pound)
